questions.q: Which Oracle Application Express component is used to learn and practice SQL?
questions.e: SQL Workshop is the component used to learn SQL. Application Builder is used to design an application, and Object Browser is a separate component; Query Optimizer is not an APEX component at all.

questions.q: Which Oracle Application Express component is used to design an application?
questions.e: Application Builder is used to design an application. SQL Workshop is for learning SQL and Object Browser is a separate component; Data Modeler is not listed as an APEX component.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of Oracle Application Express?
questions.e: The three named components are SQL Workshop, Application Builder, and Object Browser. Transaction Manager is not one of them.

questions.q: What does the statement SELECT * FROM employees; return?
o: Only the column names of the table
All the rows in the employees table
A count of the rows in the table
Only the first row of the employees table
questions.e: The SELECT * form returns all the rows in a table (across all columns). It does not restrict to the first row, return only column names, or produce a count.

questions.q: To restrict a query to a subset of rows that meet a condition, which clause must be added to the SELECT statement?
questions.e: The WHERE clause specifies the condition that limits the query to a subset of rows. FROM names the table, SELECT lists the columns, and ORDER BY only sorts results; none of these filter rows.

questions.q: Given the query SELECT first_name, last_name, job_id FROM employees WHERE job_id = 'SA_REP'; what result does it produce?
o: All rows but only the job_id column
Three named columns only for employees whose job_id is SA_REP
questions.e: The column list restricts output to first_name, last_name, and job_id, and the WHERE clause restricts rows to those where job_id equals 'SA_REP'. It is neither all columns nor all rows, and there is no sorting.

questions.q: The command 'SEECT * FROM employees;' fails. What is the cause of the error?
o: The asterisk cannot be used with FROM
The table employees does not exist
questions.e: SQL keywords must be spelled correctly; 'SEECT' is a misspelling of SELECT and produces an error. The fix is simply to correct the spelling and run again. The asterisk is valid and a WHERE clause is optional.

questions.q: An application is compared to a car with a friendly 'shell' that hides the transmission and fuel systems. What point does this analogy make about applications?
o: Applications expose all internal coding to the user
The user only needs to know enough to make the application work
Applications cannot be used without programming knowledge
Users must understand every internal system to use the application
questions.e: The car analogy illustrates that a user only needs enough knowledge to make the application work; the shell hides internal complexity, just as a driver need not understand the electrical or fuel systems. The other options contradict this hiding of complexity.

questions.q: Yahoo.com stores data in an Oracle database, yet ordinary users retrieve email with a few mouse clicks. Why do those users not need to know SQL?
o: Each user writes SQL that the browser hides
SQL is automatically generated by the operating system
The application has the SQL and other code pre-programmed into it
Oracle databases do not use SQL
questions.e: An application has all of the SQL (and other coding languages) pre-programmed into it, so users access information with a few clicks instead of learning SQL. The database still relies on SQL, and it is the application, not the OS or the user, that supplies it.

questions.q: In SQL terminology, what is the name for the portion of data returned when a query is restricted by criteria?
questions.e: A subset is the reduced portion of the data returned by criteria. Syntax refers to the rules of writing statements, a comparison operator is a symbol used in a condition, and a matrix describes the table structure.

questions.q: What term refers to the required structure and spelling rules of a SQL statement?
questions.e: Syntax is the set of rules governing how a SQL statement must be written; incorrect syntax (such as a misspelled keyword) causes errors. A subset is a filtered result, and a comparison operator is a symbol within a condition.

questions.q: In the condition WHERE job_id = 'SA_REP', which element is the comparison operator?
questions.e: The equals sign (=) is the comparison operator that tests job_id against the value 'SA_REP'. job_id is the column, 'SA_REP' is the compared value, and WHERE is the clause that introduces the condition.

questions.q: Which SELECT statement displays every column of the employees table?
questions.e: SELECT * FROM employees; displays all columns for all rows. The asterisk is the wildcard for all columns; 'columns' and 'ALL_COLUMNS' are not valid keywords, and a FROM clause naming the table is required.

questions.q: In a relational database, how is data organized?
o: As a hierarchical tree of nodes
In a network of linked pointers
In a two-dimensional matrix known as a table
questions.e: Relational data is stored in a two-dimensional matrix known as a table (rows and columns). Trees, single files, and pointer networks describe other, non-relational storage structures.

questions.q: Which software is responsible for managing the reading and manipulating of data in the tables?
questions.e: Database management system (DBMS) software manages reading and manipulating the data. The user interface hides that work, and the OS file manager or a spreadsheet does not manage relational data access.

questions.q: How is each row of data in a table uniquely identified?
questions.e: Each row can be uniquely identified by a primary key. A foreign key relates rows across tables, an index improves query performance, and a synonym is just an alternative name for an object.

questions.q: What is used to logically relate data from multiple tables?
questions.e: Foreign keys logically relate data across multiple tables by referencing a primary key. Primary keys identify rows within a table, indexes speed up queries, and synonyms only provide alternative object names.

questions.q: SQL is the standard language for operating relational databases established by which organization?
o: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
questions.e: SQL is the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard language for operating relational databases (and is also ISO SQL:1999 compliant). IEEE, W3C, and IETF standardize other domains.

questions.q: With which ISO standard is SQL described as being compliant?
questions.e: SQL is described as compliant with the ISO Standard SQL 1999. The other years correspond to different SQL revisions not cited here.

questions.q: How is SQL best characterized as a language?
questions.e: SQL is a set-based, declarative language used to access data in an Oracle database: you state what data you want, not the physical access route. It is not procedural, low-level, or object-oriented in this description.

questions.q: Which category of SQL commands contains INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE?
questions.e: DML (Data Manipulation Language) manipulates data with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. DDL defines structures, DCL controls access, and TCL manages transactions.

questions.q: Under this categorization of SQL commands, the SELECT command belongs to which category?
questions.e: Here SELECT is placed in DQL (Data Query Language), which queries/selects data, while DML is limited to INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. DDL defines structures and TCL manages transactions.

questions.q: Which category of SQL commands defines database structures?
questions.e: DDL (Data Definition Language) defines database structures such as tables. DML manipulates data, DCL controls user access, and DQL queries data.

questions.q: Which category of SQL commands controls user access to the database?
questions.e: DCL (Data Control Language) controls user access. TCL manages transactions, DQL selects data, and DDL defines structures.

questions.q: Which category of SQL commands manages database transactions?
questions.e: TCL (Transactional Control Language) manages database transactions. DCL controls access, DML manipulates data, and DQL queries data.

questions.q: Which of the following is a stage of SQL processing?
questions.e: Row Source Generation is one of the SQL processing stages, along with Parsing, Optimization, and Execution. Normalization, indexing, and machine-code compilation are not listed stages of SQL processing.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the stages of SQL processing?
o: Parsing, Optimization, Row Source Generation, Execution
Optimization, Parsing, Execution, Row Source Generation
Row Source Generation, Parsing, Optimization, Execution
Execution, Parsing, Optimization, Row Source Generation
questions.e: The stages proceed Parsing, then Optimization, then Row Source Generation, then Execution. The other orderings misplace one or more stages.

questions.q: Specialized tools installed on users' computers that send SQL commands to the Oracle Database server are called what?
questions.e: These tools are called clients; they send SQL instructions to the server. The server receives and processes the commands, while drivers and daemons refer to other software roles.

questions.q: Which of the following is named as a client tool for accessing the Oracle Database server?
questions.e: SQL*Plus is named as a client tool used to send SQL commands to the Oracle Database server. Excel, Notepad, and MySQL Workbench are not identified as Oracle client tools here.

questions.q: Which statement is true about accessing data in a relational database?
o: You must specify the physical access route to the tables
You must know the exact disk location of each row
You must write procedural code to navigate the data
You do not specify the access route and need not know how data is arranged physically
questions.e: In a relational database you do not specify the access route to the tables and do not need to know how the data is arranged physically; you simply execute a SQL statement. The other options describe the physical navigation that SQL deliberately abstracts away.

questions.q: Which of the following is a function of SQL?
questions.e: SQL's functions include guaranteeing database consistency and integrity, along with defining objects, manipulating rows, querying data, and controlling access. Disk formatting, Java compilation, and OS management are outside SQL's role.

questions.q: Which database object is the basic unit of storage and consists of rows?
questions.e: A table is the basic unit of storage and consists of rows. A view logically represents subsets of data, a sequence generates numeric values, and an index improves query performance.

questions.q: Which database object logically represents subsets of data from one or more tables?
questions.e: A view logically represents subsets of data from one or more tables. An index improves performance, a synonym provides an alternative name, and a sequence generates numeric values.

questions.q: Which database object generates numeric values?
questions.e: A sequence generates numeric values. An index improves query performance, a view represents data subsets, and a synonym gives an alternative name to an object.

questions.q: Which database object is used to improve the performance of some queries?
questions.e: An index improves the performance of some queries. A synonym provides an alternative name, a view represents subsets of data, and a sequence generates numeric values.

questions.q: Which database object gives an alternative name to an object?
questions.e: A synonym gives an alternative name to an object. A sequence generates numeric values, an index improves performance, and a view represents subsets of data.

questions.q: Under Oracle's rules for naming tables and columns, a name must begin with which of the following?
questions.e: Table and column names must begin with a letter. Although digits, underscore, dollar sign, and # may appear elsewhere in the name, they cannot be the first character.

questions.q: What is the permitted length range for table and column names?
questions.e: Table and column names must be 1 to 30 characters long. The other ranges do not match the stated rule.

questions.q: Which of the following characters is NOT permitted within a table or column name?
questions.e: Names may contain only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, underscore (_), dollar sign ($), and number sign (#). A hyphen is not among the allowed characters.

questions.q: After issuing a CREATE TABLE statement, which command confirms the table was created and displays its structure?
questions.e: The DESCRIBE command confirms table creation and shows its columns, data types, and lengths. SHOW, LIST, and DISPLAY are not the commands used for this purpose.

questions.q: Which data type stores variable-length character data, requires a maximum size to be specified, and has a maximum size of 32767 bytes?
questions.e: VARCHAR2(size) is variable-length character data with a required maximum size and a maximum of 32767 bytes. CHAR is fixed-length (max 2000 bytes), LONG is variable-length up to 2 GB, and DATE stores date/time values.

questions.q: What is the maximum size of a CHAR(size) column?
questions.e: CHAR is fixed-length character data with a maximum size of 2,000 bytes (default and minimum size is 1). 32,767 bytes is the VARCHAR2 maximum, not CHAR's.

questions.q: In the data type NUMBER(p, s), what does the scale (s) represent?
o: The number of digits to the right of the decimal point
The total number of decimal digits
The number of bytes used for storage
questions.e: In NUMBER(p, s), scale (s) is the number of digits to the right of the decimal point, while precision (p) is the total number of decimal digits. Scale is not a byte count or a maximum value.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the DEFAULT option in a CREATE TABLE statement, as in hire_date DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE?
o: It makes the column a primary key
It prevents null values from entering the column when a row is inserted without a value for it
It creates a foreign key reference
It forces the column to reject all inserts
questions.e: The DEFAULT option supplies a value so that null values do not enter the column when a row is inserted without a value for that column. It does not reject inserts, define a primary key, or create a foreign key.

questions.q: Which of the following is an ILLEGAL value for a column's DEFAULT option?
o: A SQL function such as SYSDATE
questions.e: Literal values, expressions, and SQL functions are legal defaults, but another column's name (or a pseudocolumn) is an illegal default value. The default's data type must also match the column's data type.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid integrity constraint type?
questions.e: The valid constraint types are NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK. DEFAULT is a column option, not a constraint type.

questions.q: Which constraint can be defined ONLY at the column level and not at the table level?
questions.e: A NOT NULL constraint can be defined only at the column level. Primary key, foreign key, and composite unique constraints that span multiple columns must be defined at the table level.

questions.q: A primary key made up of more than one column (a composite primary key) must be created at which level?
questions.e: A composite primary key must be created at the table level, because constraints applying to more than one column must be defined there. A single-column key may be defined at the column level.

questions.q: Which statement about the UNIQUE constraint is correct?
o: It automatically makes the column a primary key
Only one UNIQUE constraint is allowed per table
It enables the input of nulls, and a null always satisfies the constraint
It prohibits null values in the column
questions.e: A UNIQUE constraint enables the input of nulls; a null in the column (or in all columns of a composite unique key) always satisfies the constraint. It does not prohibit nulls, is not limited to one per table, and does not create a primary key.

questions.q: What must be true of the value(s) in a column defined as a PRIMARY KEY?
o: Not null but duplicates are allowed
Only that the value is not null
Both unique AND not null for all rows
questions.e: A PRIMARY KEY requires values to be both unique and not null for every row. UNIQUE alone permits nulls, and NOT NULL alone permits duplicates; the primary key enforces both conditions.

questions.q: For a FOREIGN KEY constraint, what must a foreign key value do?
o: Match an existing value in the parent table or be NULL
Never be NULL under any circumstance
Match the primary key of the same row
Always be unique across the child table
questions.e: A foreign key value must match an existing value in the parent table or be NULL. It need not be unique in the child table, may be null, and references the parent table's key rather than its own row.

questions.q: What does the ON DELETE CASCADE keyword do in a foreign key constraint?
o: Sets dependent foreign key values to null
Deletes the dependent rows in the child table when a row in the parent table is deleted
Copies the parent row into the child table
Prevents a parent row from being deleted while children exist
questions.e: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the dependent (child) rows when the referenced parent row is deleted. Converting dependent values to null is done by ON DELETE SET NULL, not CASCADE.

questions.q: What does the ON DELETE SET NULL keyword do in a foreign key constraint?
o: Blocks the deletion of the parent row
Resets the foreign key to its default value
Converts the dependent foreign key values to null
Deletes the child rows along with the parent row
questions.e: ON DELETE SET NULL converts the dependent foreign key values to null when the parent row is deleted. Deleting the child rows is the behavior of ON DELETE CASCADE.

questions.q: Which statement is true of a CHECK constraint?
o: It automatically enforces a NOT NULL rule
It generates numeric values for a column
It can reference columns from other tables
It defines a condition that each row must satisfy and cannot reference columns from other tables
questions.e: A CHECK constraint defines a condition that each row must satisfy and cannot reference columns from other tables. It does not by itself enforce NOT NULL and does not generate values.

questions.q: Which DDL statement is used to modify an existing object's structure, such as adding or dropping a column?
questions.e: ALTER is the DDL statement used to modify an object's structure (for example, ALTER TABLE ... ADD/MODIFY/DROP). UPDATE and INSERT are DML commands that change data, not structure, and MODIFY is a clause within ALTER TABLE, not a standalone statement.

questions.q: When a table is dropped with DROP TABLE dept; (without the PURGE clause), what happens to the table?
o: It is permanently erased immediately with no recovery
It is moved to the recycle bin
It is set to read-only mode
It is converted into a view
questions.e: DROP TABLE moves the table to the recycle bin; the table and its data are removed permanently only if the PURGE clause is specified. It is not converted to a view or merely made read-only.

questions.q: Which DML statement is used to remove existing rows from a table?
questions.e: DELETE removes existing rows from a table. INSERT adds new rows, UPDATE modifies existing rows, and SELECT only retrieves data without changing it.

questions.q: A collection of DML statements that form a logical unit of work is called a:
questions.e: A transaction is a collection of DML statements that form a logical unit of work. A constraint enforces data rules, a savepoint marks a point within a transaction, and a schema is a collection of database objects.

questions.q: Using the basic INSERT ... VALUES syntax, how many rows are added by a single statement?
o: Exactly one row at a time
As many rows as the table already contains
An unlimited number in one VALUES list
All rows from a copied table
questions.e: With the standard INSERT INTO ... VALUES syntax, only one row is inserted at a time. Inserting many rows would require a different technique such as a subquery, not multiple values in one VALUES clause.

questions.q: When you insert a row that supplies a value for every column of a table, the column list in the INSERT clause is:
o: Required only if the table has a primary key
questions.e: If you provide a value for each column, the column list is not required; the values are matched to the columns in their default table order. The list is only needed when you supply values for a subset of columns or in a non-default order.

questions.q: In an INSERT statement that omits the column list, in what order must the values be provided?
o: Order of the primary key first, then the rest
The default order of the columns in the table
Any order, because Oracle matches by data type
questions.e: When the column list is omitted, values must be listed in the default order of the columns in the table. Oracle does not reorder them by name, key, or data type, so a wrong order assigns values to the wrong columns.

questions.q: When inserting data, character and date values must be enclosed within:
questions.e: Character and date values must be enclosed within single quotation marks in the VALUES clause. Double quotation marks are used for column aliases, not literal data values.

questions.q: Which describes the EXPLICIT method of inserting a NULL value into a column?
o: Specify the NULL keyword in the VALUES clause
Enclose an empty string in single quotes
Use the SYSDATE function in that position
Omit the column from the column list
questions.e: The explicit method omits the column entirely from the column list so no value is supplied. The implicit method instead names the column and places the NULL keyword in the VALUES clause.

questions.q: Which function records the current date and time when used in an INSERT statement?
questions.e: SYSDATE records the current date and time. TO_DATE converts a character string into a specific date value rather than returning the current moment.

questions.q: When you copy a table using CREATE TABLE copy_departments AS (SELECT * FROM departments), which constraints are copied?
questions.e: Copying a table with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies only the NOT NULL constraints. Primary key, foreign key, and check constraints are not carried over to the new table.

questions.q: What is the effect of running an UPDATE statement that has no WHERE clause?
o: Only the first row is changed
All rows in the table are modified
questions.e: If the WHERE clause is omitted, the values for all rows in the table are modified. The WHERE clause is what restricts the change to a specific row or set of rows.

questions.q: To change an existing column value to NULL with an UPDATE statement, you would write:
questions.e: You specify SET column_name = NULL to update a column value to NULL. Setting it to 0 or an empty string stores those literal values, which are not the same as NULL.

questions.q: In an UPDATE statement, which keyword introduces the new column values?
questions.e: UPDATE uses the SET keyword to assign new column values (SET column = value). VALUES and INTO belong to the INSERT statement.

questions.q: To identify a single row for an UPDATE, which column is generally recommended in the WHERE clause?
o: The last column in the table
questions.e: Using the primary key column in the WHERE clause identifies a single row uniquely for update. Other columns may match multiple rows and unintentionally update more than one.

questions.q: An UPDATE sets department_id = 55 where department_id = 110, but department 55 does not exist in the parent DEPARTMENTS table. What happens?
o: The statement violates an integrity (foreign key) constraint
The update succeeds but is automatically rolled back later
The rows are updated and 55 is added to DEPARTMENTS
All rows are set to NULL instead
questions.e: Because 55 does not exist in the parent DEPARTMENTS table, the update violates the foreign key integrity constraint and fails. Oracle does not auto-create the missing parent value or silently substitute NULL.

questions.q: In the DELETE statement syntax DELETE [FROM] table [WHERE condition], which keyword is optional?
questions.e: The FROM keyword is optional in the DELETE syntax (shown by the brackets around it). The WHERE clause is also optional, but omitting it deletes every row rather than being an APEX-specific behavior.

questions.q: What is the result of DELETE FROM copy_departments; with no WHERE clause?
o: All rows in the table are deleted
Only rows with NULL values are deleted
Nothing is deleted without a WHERE clause
questions.e: Omitting the WHERE clause deletes all rows in the table. The table structure remains; only DROP removes the table itself.

questions.q: Why can a DELETE fail when removing a row such as the one with department_id = 60?
o: The row contains a NULL value
Only TRUNCATE can remove that row
Its primary key is used as a foreign key in another table
questions.e: You cannot delete a row whose primary key is used as a foreign key in another (child) table, because doing so would break referential integrity. NULL values and missing WHERE clauses do not cause this particular failure.

questions.q: The TRUNCATE statement is classified as which type of statement?
questions.e: TRUNCATE is a DDL statement, not a DML statement, and therefore cannot easily be undone. DELETE, by contrast, is DML and can be rolled back before a commit.

questions.q: What does the TRUNCATE TABLE statement do?
o: Removes all rows and also drops the table structure
Removes only rows that violate constraints
Removes all rows but leaves the table structure intact
questions.e: TRUNCATE TABLE removes all rows from a table, leaving the table empty but the table structure intact. It does not drop the table, and unlike DELETE it is a DDL operation that cannot easily be undone.

questions.q: A student wants to delete every row of a table but keep its structure, and wants an operation that cannot easily be undone. Which statement fits best?
questions.e: TRUNCATE TABLE empties the table while keeping the structure and, being DDL, cannot easily be undone. DELETE would also empty the table but as DML it can be rolled back, and DROP TABLE removes the structure entirely.

questions.q: Which function is used to insert a specific literal date value such as December 7, 2002 into a table?
questions.e: TO_DATE('Dec 7, 2002', 'MON DD, YYYY') converts a character string to a specific date using a format model. SYSDATE would insert the current date and time instead of the chosen date.

questions.q: Which sequence of DML operations correctly reflects the three core table-data operations of DML?
questions.e: The core DML operations for managing a table's data are INSERT (add rows), UPDATE (modify rows), and DELETE (remove rows). CREATE/ALTER/DROP are DDL and GRANT/REVOKE are DCL.

questions.q: Why are COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT not supported in Oracle Application Express?
o: Because they were replaced by TRUNCATE
Because of the way Oracle Application Express manages connections to the database
Because APEX does not use transactions at all
questions.e: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT are not supported in Oracle Application Express because of the way APEX manages its connections to the database. APEX still uses transactions internally; it simply does not let users control them with these explicit statements.

questions.q: Which TCL statement ends the current transaction by making all pending data changes permanent?
questions.e: COMMIT ends the current transaction by making all pending data changes permanent. ROLLBACK instead discards pending changes, and SAVEPOINT only marks a point within the transaction.

questions.q: Which statement ends the current transaction by discarding all pending data changes?
questions.e: ROLLBACK (without a TO SAVEPOINT clause) ends the current transaction by discarding all pending data changes. COMMIT would instead make them permanent.

questions.q: What does the SAVEPOINT statement do?
o: Marks a savepoint within the current transaction
questions.e: SAVEPOINT marks a named savepoint within the current transaction so you can later roll back to it. It does not commit or discard changes by itself.

questions.q: When you issue ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT B, what happens to changes and savepoints made after savepoint B?
o: Only savepoints are kept, changes are discarded
They are moved to a new transaction
questions.e: ROLLBACK TO a savepoint discards any changes and savepoints that were created after the savepoint to which you are rolling back. Everything before that savepoint remains pending.

questions.q: If you issue ROLLBACK and omit the TO SAVEPOINT clause, what is rolled back?
o: Only changes since the most recent savepoint
questions.e: If you omit the TO SAVEPOINT clause, the ROLLBACK statement rolls back the entire transaction. Naming a savepoint would limit the rollback to changes made after that savepoint.

questions.q: Which statement about savepoints is true?
o: Savepoints are logical, so there is no way to list the savepoints you created
A transaction may contain only one savepoint
You can query a list of all savepoints you created
questions.e: Because savepoints are logical, there is no way to list the savepoints that you have created. A transaction can contain multiple savepoints, and they are not committed on their own.

questions.q: When does a database transaction begin?
o: When the first DML SQL statement is executed
When you log in to the database
questions.e: A transaction begins when the first DML SQL statement is executed. COMMIT and ROLLBACK end transactions rather than start them, and logging in alone starts no transaction.

questions.q: Which of the following ends a transaction with an automatic commit?
o: Executing a DDL or TCL statement
questions.e: When a DDL or TCL statement executes, the current transaction ends with an automatic commit. Additional DML statements simply continue the same transaction, and a plain SELECT does not commit.

questions.q: An automatic rollback occurs under which circumstance?
o: A normal exit from the SQL software
An abnormal termination of the SQL software or a system failure
questions.e: An automatic rollback occurs when there is an abnormal termination of the SQL software or a system failure, protecting database integrity. A normal exit or a DDL statement instead causes an automatic commit.

questions.q: A single database transaction can consist of which of the following?
o: Any number of DDL statements plus one DML statement
DML statements representing one consistent change, or one DDL statement, or one TCL statement
Only a mixture of DML and DCL statements
questions.e: A database transaction consists of either DML statements that represent one consistent change to the data, or one DDL statement, or one TCL statement. Multiple DDL statements are not grouped into a single transaction because each DDL auto-commits.

questions.q: Before a COMMIT or ROLLBACK, which sessions can view the results of the current session's DML operations?
o: Only sessions with the same user name
No session, not even the current one
questions.e: Before a commit, only the current session can review the pending DML results (using SELECT); other sessions cannot see them. The affected rows are also locked so other sessions cannot change them.

questions.q: During an uncommitted transaction, what happens to the rows affected by the DML operations?
o: They are locked so other sessions cannot change them
They are visible to all sessions immediately
They are unlocked and freely editable by anyone
questions.e: The affected rows are locked so that other sessions cannot change the data in those rows until the transaction ends. The changes remain invisible to other sessions until a commit is issued.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the data state after a COMMIT?
o: The previous state of the data can still be recovered
Data changes are saved in the database
Locks on the affected rows are released
questions.e: After a COMMIT, the previous state is overwritten and cannot be recovered. The other statements are all true: changes are saved, locks are released, and all savepoints are erased.

questions.q: After a ROLLBACK statement is issued, what happens to the data?
o: Changes become permanent and locks stay held
Only savepoints are erased while changes remain
Data changes are undone, the previous state is restored, and locks are released
questions.e: After a ROLLBACK, data changes are undone, the previous state of the data is restored, and locks on the affected rows are released. This is the opposite of COMMIT, which makes changes permanent.

questions.q: Read consistency guarantees that each user sees data as it existed as of which point in time?
o: The moment the database was created
The start of the current session
questions.e: Read consistency guarantees a consistent view of the data, so each user sees data as it existed as of the last COMMIT. Uncommitted changes made by other sessions are not visible.

questions.q: According to read consistency rules, which of the following is TRUE?
questions.e: Under read consistency, readers do not wait for writers and writers do not wait for readers, but writers do wait for other writers on the same data. This lets queries and updates proceed without blocking each other except when two writers target the same rows.

questions.q: If a single DML statement fails during execution, what happens?
o: The entire transaction is rolled back
Only that statement is rolled back and all other changes are retained
questions.e: With a statement-level rollback, if one DML statement fails, only that statement is rolled back via an implicit savepoint the Oracle server creates, and all other changes are retained. The user should still end the transaction explicitly with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of using COMMIT and ROLLBACK statements?
o: They remove the need for a WHERE clause
They let you preview data changes before making them permanent
questions.e: COMMIT and ROLLBACK let you ensure data consistency, preview data changes before making them permanent, group logically related operations, and control permanent changes. They do not create indexes or change statement types.

questions.q: When one user updates a row and has not yet committed, how does the Oracle server provide other users a consistent view of that data?
o: It returns NULL for the affected column
It uses undo (rollback) segments to show the before-change image of the data
It blocks all readers until the writer commits
It returns the changed, uncommitted value
questions.e: The Oracle server uses undo segments to reconstruct the before-change (old) image, so other users get a read-consistent view as of the last commit. Readers are not blocked by the writer, and they never see the uncommitted new value.

questions.q: A transaction that transfers funds must debit one account and credit another for the same amount, and both must fail or succeed together. This requirement illustrates:
o: A transaction as one consistent, all-or-nothing change to the data
questions.e: The funds-transfer example illustrates that a transaction represents one consistent change where all actions succeed or fail together, so the credit is never committed without the debit. Read consistency and statement-level rollback are related but separate concepts.

questions.q: In a SELECT statement, what do the SELECT and FROM keywords identify?
o: SELECT identifies the table; FROM identifies the columns
SELECT identifies the columns to display; FROM identifies the table containing them
questions.e: SELECT identifies the columns to be displayed, and FROM identifies the table that contains those columns. Reversing their roles would make the statement invalid.

questions.q: How do you display all columns of a table in a query?
o: Use the keyword ALL after SELECT
Place an asterisk (*) after the SELECT keyword
questions.e: Placing an asterisk (*) after SELECT displays all columns of the table. DISTINCT eliminates duplicate rows, and ALL is not the mechanism used to select every column here.

questions.q: Selecting only specific columns of a table by naming them in the SELECT clause is known as:
questions.e: Choosing specific columns is called projection. Selection refers to choosing specific rows (via a WHERE condition), and joining combines data from multiple tables.

questions.q: Arithmetic operators can be used in any clause of a SQL statement EXCEPT which one?
questions.e: Arithmetic operators can be used in any clause except the FROM clause, which only names the source table(s). They are allowed in SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY.

questions.q: For the expression 12*salary+100 where salary is 24000, what value is returned?
questions.e: By operator precedence, multiplication happens before addition: 12*24000 = 288000, then +100 = 288100. Adding first (24000+100 then *12) would give 289200, which requires parentheses.

questions.q: For the expression 12*(salary+100) where salary is 24000, what value is returned?
questions.e: Parentheses override precedence, so salary+100 = 24100 is evaluated first, then 12*24100 = 289200. Without the parentheses (12*salary+100) the result would be 288100.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a NULL value?
o: It is the same as zero
It is a value that is unavailable, unassigned, unknown, or inapplicable
It is the same as a blank space
It is only allowed in date columns
questions.e: A null is a value that is unavailable, unassigned, unknown, or inapplicable, and it is not the same as zero or a blank space. Zero and blank are actual stored values, whereas null represents the absence of a value.

questions.q: What is the result of an arithmetic expression such as 12*salary*commission_pct when commission_pct is NULL?
questions.e: Any arithmetic expression containing a null value evaluates to null. So if commission_pct is null, the whole product is null rather than zero or the partial result.

questions.q: Which statement about a column alias is TRUE?
o: It renames a column heading and may optionally use the AS keyword
It can only be used on NUMBER columns
It changes the actual column name in the table
It must always be enclosed in single quotes
questions.e: A column alias renames a column heading, is useful with calculations, and may optionally use the AS keyword between the column and the alias. It does not alter the stored column name, and it uses double quotes (not single) only when it contains spaces or is case-sensitive.

questions.q: When does a column alias require enclosure in double quotation marks?
o: When it contains spaces or special characters or must be case-sensitive
Only when used with the AS keyword
Only when the alias is a single word
questions.e: Double quotation marks are required for an alias that contains spaces or special characters, or that must be case-sensitive, because by default aliases are displayed in all uppercase. A simple one-word uppercase alias needs no quotes.

questions.q: By default, how do column headings appear in query output?
o: Exactly as typed in the SELECT clause
questions.e: Column names appear in uppercase by default. To preserve mixed case or spaces in a heading, you must enclose the alias in double quotation marks.

questions.q: The concatenation operator in SQL is represented by:
questions.e: The concatenation operator is represented by two vertical bars (||). It links columns or character strings together and creates a column that is a character expression, unlike + which performs arithmetic addition.

questions.q: What is the result of concatenating a NULL with a character string using the || operator?
questions.e: Concatenating a NULL with a character value results in a character string (the character portion is returned). This differs from arithmetic, where a NULL operand makes the whole expression null.

questions.q: A literal character or date value included in a SELECT list must be:
questions.e: Date and character literal values must be enclosed within single quotation marks. Double quotation marks are reserved for column aliases, and each literal string is output once for every row returned.

questions.q: When a literal string itself contains a single quotation mark (for example Department's), which feature lets you choose your own delimiter such as brackets?
questions.e: The alternative quote (q) operator, written as q'[ ... ]', lets you pick your own delimiter so a single quote inside the literal (like Department's) does not end the string prematurely. Concatenation and DISTINCT serve unrelated purposes.

questions.q: Which keyword eliminates duplicate rows from a query result, and where is it placed?
o: UNIQUE, placed in the FROM clause
DISTINCT, placed immediately after the SELECT keyword
DISTINCT, placed at the end of the statement
NODUP, placed after the table name
questions.e: The DISTINCT keyword eliminates duplicate rows and must be placed immediately after the SELECT keyword. Without it, the default display returns all rows, including duplicates.

questions.q: By default (without DISTINCT), how does a query display rows?
o: It displays all rows, including duplicate rows
It displays only the first occurrence of each row
questions.e: The default display of queries is all rows, including duplicate rows. Duplicates are only removed when the DISTINCT keyword is added after SELECT.

questions.q: Which command displays the structure of a table, including column name, data type, and nullability?
questions.e: The DESCRIBE (abbreviated DESC) command displays a table's structure, including column name, data type, and nullability. SELECT * returns the data rows, not the structural definition.

questions.q: Which statement about writing SQL statements is TRUE?
o: Keywords cannot be abbreviated or split across lines
Keywords can be abbreviated to save typing
Each statement must be written on a single line
questions.e: Keywords cannot be abbreviated or split across lines and are typically written in uppercase. SQL statements themselves are not case-sensitive and may span one or more lines.

questions.q: In Oracle Application Express, terminating a SQL statement with a semicolon (;) is:
questions.e: In Application Express, SQL statements can be terminated by a semicolon, but it is not mandatory. This is a convenience of the APEX environment rather than a universal SQL rule.

questions.q: Using an alias, the expression salary*12 with the heading "Annual Salary" returns what value for a salary of 24000?
questions.e: Multiplying salary 24000 by 12 gives 288000, displayed under the double-quoted alias "Annual Salary" to preserve the space and case. The other values do not result from 24000*12.

questions.q: Which list correctly names the four arithmetic operators available for building expressions in a SELECT statement?
questions.e: The arithmetic operators are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), and / (divide). The || symbol is the concatenation operator, not an arithmetic one, and AS introduces an alias.

questions.q: In relational algebra, the result of applying any operation is always:
questions.e: Every relational algebra operation produces a new relation, formed from one or more input relations. This is the 'closed' property of the algebra: all objects it manipulates are relations, so results can be further operated upon by the same algebra. The distractors describe outputs (scalar, columns, Boolean) that would violate closure.

questions.q: Which operation selects a subset of the TUPLES (rows) of a relation that satisfy a Boolean condition, while keeping all attributes?
questions.e: SELECT (σ) filters rows using a Boolean selection condition and returns a relation with the same schema (all attributes) as the input. PROJECT keeps chosen columns and drops others; RENAME changes names; CARTESIAN PRODUCT combines two relations. Only SELECT does horizontal filtering of tuples.

questions.q: A cascade of several SELECT operations applied one after another to a relation R can always be replaced by:
o: A single SELECT whose condition is the AND (conjunction) of all the individual conditions
A single PROJECT of the listed attributes
A CARTESIAN PRODUCT of the conditions
A UNION of the individual results
questions.e: Because SELECT conditions are conjunctive filters, σc1(σc2(σc3(R))) equals σ(c1 AND c2 AND c3)(R). The other options confuse SELECT with PROJECT, CARTESIAN PRODUCT, or UNION, which do not combine row filters into one conjunction.

questions.q: The PROJECT operation π<list>(R) automatically removes duplicate tuples from its result because:
o: Duplicates would slow the query down
The projected attributes are always keys
The result of PROJECT must be a set, and sets contain no duplicate elements
questions.e: PROJECT keeps only the listed columns, which can create duplicate rows; these are removed because a relation is a mathematical set and sets do not allow duplicate elements. Speed and keys are not the reason; SELECT filters rows, not duplicate columns.

questions.q: The number of tuples in the result of PROJECT π<list>(R) equals the number of tuples in R exactly when:
o: R has no duplicate tuples anywhere
The list contains a single attribute
The list of attributes includes a key of R
questions.e: PROJECT normally yields a count less than or equal to |R| because duplicates are removed; but if the projection list includes a key of R, every projected row is unique, so the count equals |R|. A single non-key attribute could still collapse into duplicates.

questions.q: Which pair of properties correctly describes SELECT versus PROJECT?
o: SELECT is not commutative; PROJECT is commutative
SELECT is commutative; PROJECT is NOT commutative
questions.e: SELECT is commutative (its row filters can be reordered), whereas PROJECT is not commutative because reordering projection lists can drop attributes needed by a later projection. This is a classic point of confusion between the two unary operations.

questions.q: The RENAME operator (ρ) is used to:
o: Change the relation name and/or the attribute names of a relation
questions.e: RENAME (ρ) changes the relation name, the attribute names, or both. It is often necessary before a JOIN when attributes must be given matching or distinct names. It does not filter tuples (SELECT) or remove duplicates (PROJECT).

questions.q: For the UNION, INTERSECTION, and SET DIFFERENCE operations, the two operand relations must be type (UNION) compatible, meaning they must have:
o: The same number of attributes with corresponding attributes drawn from compatible domains
questions.e: Type (UNION) compatibility requires the same number of attributes and pairwise-compatible domains (dom(Ai)=dom(Bi)); the attribute NAMES need not match. Equal tuple counts or a shared key are not required.

questions.q: The result of R ∪ S is a relation containing:
o: All tuples that are in R, in S, or in both, with duplicates eliminated
Only tuples that appear in both R and S
Tuples in R but not in S
Every combination of a tuple from R with a tuple from S
questions.e: UNION returns all tuples in R or S or both, eliminating duplicates. Tuples in both only is INTERSECTION; R but not S is SET DIFFERENCE; every combination is CARTESIAN PRODUCT.

questions.q: Which set operation returns exactly the tuples that appear in BOTH operand relations?
questions.e: INTERSECTION (∩) returns tuples present in both R and S. UNION returns those in either; SET DIFFERENCE returns those in R but not S; CARTESIAN PRODUCT pairs tuples combinatorially.

questions.q: Which of the following relational operations is NOT commutative?
questions.e: SET DIFFERENCE is not commutative: in general R − S ≠ S − R. UNION and INTERSECTION are both commutative and associative. This asymmetry mirrors ordinary subtraction versus addition.

questions.q: If relation R has n attributes and |R| tuples, and S has m attributes and |S| tuples, then R × S (CARTESIAN PRODUCT) has:
questions.e: CARTESIAN PRODUCT produces a relation of degree n+m (all attributes of both, in order) with one tuple for every combination, giving |R|*|S| tuples. It does not require type compatibility and, unlike JOIN, applies no condition.

questions.q: Which statement about CARTESIAN PRODUCT (×) is correct?
o: The operands need NOT be type compatible, and the product alone is generally not a meaningful operation
The two operands must be type compatible
It always produces fewer tuples than either operand
It removes attributes common to both relations
questions.e: CARTESIAN PRODUCT does not require type compatibility and by itself is generally not meaningful; it becomes useful when followed by a SELECT to keep only related combinations. Type compatibility is required only for set operations.

questions.q: The JOIN operation is equivalent to which combination of more basic operations?
o: A PROJECT followed by a SELECT
A UNION followed by a PROJECT
A CARTESIAN PRODUCT followed by a SELECT
A RENAME followed by a CARTESIAN PRODUCT
questions.e: A JOIN is exactly a CARTESIAN PRODUCT followed by a SELECT on the join condition, combined into a single, commonly used operation that keeps only related tuples. The other combinations do not reproduce JOIN semantics.

questions.q: A JOIN whose join condition (theta) may be any general Boolean comparison, such as R.Ai < S.Bj, is called a:
questions.e: The general case of JOIN with an arbitrary comparison condition theta is the theta-join. An EQUIJOIN restricts theta to equality (=) comparisons only; NATURAL JOIN further removes the superfluous duplicate attribute; OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched tuples.

questions.q: An EQUIJOIN is characterized by the fact that:
o: It removes the superfluous duplicate attribute automatically
It keeps unmatched tuples padded with NULLs
It uses only equality (=) comparisons in the join condition and leaves a superfluous pair of identical-valued attributes in the result
It requires the two relations to be type compatible
questions.e: An EQUIJOIN uses only equality comparisons, and its result always contains one or more pairs of attributes holding identical values in every tuple (one being superfluous). Removing that superfluous attribute is what distinguishes NATURAL JOIN; padding unmatched tuples is OUTER JOIN.

questions.q: How does NATURAL JOIN (*) differ from EQUIJOIN?
o: NATURAL JOIN keeps both copies of the join attribute; EQUIJOIN keeps one
NATURAL JOIN allows any comparison operator; EQUIJOIN allows only <
NATURAL JOIN removes the superfluous (duplicate) join attribute and matches attributes of the same name; EQUIJOIN retains it
NATURAL JOIN requires type compatibility; EQUIJOIN does not
questions.e: NATURAL JOIN (*) was created to remove the superfluous second attribute produced by an EQUIJOIN, and it implicitly equates attributes having the same name in both relations (renaming first if names differ). EQUIJOIN keeps the redundant matched pair.

questions.q: Which of the following is the recognized COMPLETE SET of relational algebra operations, from which all others can be derived?
o: {SELECT, PROJECT, UNION, SET DIFFERENCE, RENAME, CARTESIAN PRODUCT}
questions.e: The complete set is {SELECT, PROJECT, UNION, SET DIFFERENCE, RENAME, CARTESIAN PRODUCT}; any other expression (e.g., INTERSECTION, JOIN) can be built from these. For instance R∩S = (R∪S)−((R−S)∪(S−R)), and JOIN = SELECT applied to a CARTESIAN PRODUCT.

questions.q: The DIVISION operation R(Z) ÷ S(X), where X ⊆ Z and Y = Z − X, returns a relation T(Y) containing a tuple t such that:
o: t appears in at least one tuple of R
t appears in both R and S
t is the union of all Y-values in R
the values in t appear in R combined with EVERY tuple of S
questions.e: DIVISION returns Y-values that are associated in R with every tuple of S; that is, t qualifies only if it appears in R in combination with all S tuples. This models 'for all' queries (e.g., employees who work on all specified projects).

questions.q: Regarding the aggregate COUNT function, which statement is correct?
o: COUNT just counts the number of rows, without removing duplicates
COUNT removes duplicate values before counting
COUNT can only be applied to key attributes
COUNT returns the sum of numeric values
questions.e: COUNT counts the number of rows (tuples/values) and does not remove duplicates. SUM adds numeric values, and MAX/MIN/AVERAGE compute the corresponding summaries; none is restricted to keys.

questions.q: In the aggregate-function operation used for grouping, written as <grouping attributes> ℱ <aggregate functions> (R), the grouping attributes and the aggregate functions are placed:
o: Both to the right of ℱ
Grouping attributes to the LEFT of ℱ and aggregate functions to the RIGHT
Both to the left of ℱ
Grouping attributes to the right and aggregate functions to the left
questions.e: In the grouping-with-aggregation notation, the grouping attributes are written to the left of the ℱ symbol and the aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVERAGE, etc.) to its right. For example, DNO ℱ COUNT SSN, AVERAGE Salary groups employees by department.

questions.q: Recursive closure operations (e.g., retrieving all supervisees of an employee at every level) are notable because they:
o: Cannot in general be specified in basic relational algebra without a looping mechanism; SQL3 adds syntax for them
Are a special case of CARTESIAN PRODUCT
questions.e: Recursive closure over a recursive relationship cannot in general be expressed in basic relational algebra without looping; the SQL3 standard adds explicit syntax for recursive closure. Taking a union of levels works only for a fixed known number of levels.

questions.q: In a LEFT OUTER JOIN of R and S, a tuple of R that has no matching tuple in S is:
o: Duplicated for every tuple of S
Kept in the result, with the S attributes padded with NULL values
questions.e: LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every tuple of the left relation R; when no match exists in S, the S attributes are padded with NULLs. This avoids the information loss that ordinary NATURAL/EQUI JOIN causes by dropping unmatched tuples. RIGHT and FULL outer joins preserve S, or both, respectively.

questions.q: The OUTER UNION operation was developed to:
o: Take the union of two fully type-compatible relations faster
Remove duplicate tuples from a single relation
Take the union of two relations that are only PARTIALLY compatible, keeping shared attributes once and non-shared attributes from both
Join two relations on a common key
questions.e: OUTER UNION handles partially compatible relations R(X,Y) and S(X,Z): the shared (type-compatible) attributes X appear once, while the non-compatible attributes Y and Z from each relation are also kept, with NULLs where values are absent. It is not for fully compatible relations or plain deduplication.

questions.q: Which statement best contrasts relational algebra with relational calculus?
o: Relational algebra is procedural (specifies HOW via a sequence of operations); relational calculus is declarative/nonprocedural (specifies only WHAT)
Relational algebra is declarative; relational calculus is procedural
questions.e: Relational algebra is procedural: it prescribes a sequence of operations (how to compute the result). Relational calculus is nonprocedural/declarative: it specifies only what information the result should contain, with no order of operations. This is their main distinguishing feature.

questions.q: A simple tuple relational calculus query has the general form {t | COND(t)}. Here t is:
o: A domain variable ranging over a single column value
A tuple variable ranging over the rows of a relation, and the result is all tuples t satisfying COND(t)
questions.e: In tuple relational calculus, t is a tuple variable that ranges over the rows (tuples) of a relation, and {t | COND(t)} yields the set of all tuples making COND(t) true. Variables ranging over single column values instead characterize DOMAIN relational calculus.

questions.q: How do the variables in DOMAIN relational calculus differ from those in TUPLE relational calculus?
o: Domain variables range over entire relations; tuple variables over single values
Domain variables range over single values from the domains of attributes (columns); tuple variables range over whole tuples (rows)
Domain variables range over rows; tuple variables range over columns
questions.e: Domain relational calculus uses variables that range over single values from attribute domains (columns), needing n domain variables for a degree-n result. Tuple calculus variables range over whole tuples (rows). Both are equivalent in expressive power to relational algebra.

questions.q: In relational calculus, a tuple variable t is said to be BOUND when:
o: It appears to the left of the bar (|)
It is quantified, i.e., it appears in an (∃t) or (∀t) clause
It ranges over a single domain
It is never used in the condition
questions.e: A variable is bound when it is quantified — appearing in an existential (∃t) or universal (∀t) clause; otherwise it is free. Only free variables should appear to the left of the bar (|) in the result specification.

questions.q: Which describes the EXISTENTIAL quantifier (∃) as opposed to the UNIVERSAL quantifier (∀)?
o: (∃t)(F) is true if F is true for EVERY tuple; (∀t)(F) is true if F is true for SOME tuple
(∃t)(F) is true if F is true for at least one (some) tuple; (∀t)(F) is true only if F is true for every tuple
Both require F to be true for every tuple
Both require F to be true for at least one tuple
questions.e: The existential quantifier (∃, 'there exists') makes (∃t)(F) true if F holds for at least one tuple. The universal quantifier (∀, 'for all') makes (∀t)(F) true only if F holds for every tuple in the universe. The distractors swap or conflate these meanings.

questions.q: The word 'algebra' is derived from the title of a book ('al-jabr'), and the word 'algorithm' is derived from the name of the same scholar. That scholar was:
questions.e: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book titled 'al-jabr,' whose Latin-translated title gave 'algebra' its name; the word 'algorithm' also originates from his name 'al-Khwarizmi.' The other mathematicians are unrelated to these etymologies.

questions.q: Which type of SQL join returns only the rows for which the join condition is satisfied in both tables?
questions.e: An INNER JOIN returns only the matching rows in both tables, i.e. only those rows for which the join condition is satisfied. A LEFT/RIGHT OUTER JOIN would additionally keep non-matching rows from one side (filling NULLs), a FULL OUTER JOIN keeps non-matching rows from both sides, and a CROSS JOIN ignores any join condition and returns the Cartesian product.

questions.q: A LEFT OUTER JOIN between Customers (left) and Orders (right) is executed. For a customer who has no matching order, what appears in the Orders columns of the result?
o: NULL values in the Orders columns
The row is excluded from the result
The customer's own values copied across
A Cartesian product of all orders
questions.e: A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching right rows; when the right (Orders) table has no matching record, the Orders columns hold NULL. The row is not excluded (that would be INNER JOIN behavior), and no values are copied or multiplied.

questions.q: Given Customers C and Orders O, which query returns the customers who have NO orders?
o: SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C INNER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId
SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C CROSS JOIN Orders O
SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C RIGHT OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE C.CustomerId IS NULL
SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C LEFT OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE O.OrderId IS NULL
questions.e: To find left-table rows without a match, use a LEFT OUTER JOIN and filter WHERE the right key IS NULL (O.OrderId IS NULL). The INNER JOIN would return only customers who DO have orders, CROSS JOIN gives the Cartesian product, and the RIGHT OUTER JOIN with C.CustomerId IS NULL finds orders without a customer instead.

questions.q: In the demo tables, the customer with CustomerId 2 named Kalpana has no order in the Orders table. Which query would return Kalpana's row (CustomerId and Name)?
o: SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C LEFT OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE O.OrderId IS NULL
SELECT C.CustomerId, C.Name FROM Customers C INNER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId
SELECT O.* FROM Customers C RIGHT OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE C.CustomerId IS NULL
SELECT * FROM Customers C CROSS JOIN Orders O
questions.e: Kalpana (CustomerId 2) is a customer with no matching order, so a LEFT OUTER JOIN keeping rows where O.OrderId IS NULL returns her. The INNER JOIN excludes her (no match), the RIGHT OUTER JOIN with C.CustomerId IS NULL finds orders lacking a customer, and CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product.

questions.q: Which join returns all rows from the RIGHT table plus matching rows from the left, putting NULL in the left-table columns when there is no left match?
questions.e: A RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the right table and the corresponding matching left rows; when the left table has no matching record, its columns are NULL. LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps all left rows instead, INNER JOIN keeps only matches, and a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself.

questions.q: An order has OrderId 200 with CustomerId 4, but no customer with CustomerId 4 exists in the Customers table. In a RIGHT OUTER JOIN of Customers (left) with Orders (right) on CustomerId, what appears for this order?
o: The Customers-table columns are NULL for that order
The order is dropped from the result
The order is duplicated for every customer
An error is raised for the missing customer
questions.e: A RIGHT OUTER JOIN keeps all right-table (Orders) rows; because CustomerId 4 has no matching customer, the Customers columns for OrderId 200 are NULL. It is not dropped (that would need INNER JOIN), not duplicated (that is CROSS JOIN), and a missing match is normal, not an error.

questions.q: A FULL OUTER JOIN is equivalent to combining which two joins?
o: LEFT OUTER JOIN + RIGHT OUTER JOIN
questions.e: FULL OUTER JOIN = LEFT OUTER JOIN + RIGHT OUTER JOIN; it returns all rows from both tables with NULLs wherever a side has no match. It is not built from CROSS, INNER, or SELF joins, which serve entirely different purposes.

questions.q: Which join returns all rows from BOTH tables, placing NULLs for the columns of whichever side has no matching row?
questions.e: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns every row from both tables, using NULLs where either side lacks a match. INNER JOIN keeps only matches, CROSS JOIN gives the Cartesian product with no NULL-filling, and RIGHT OUTER JOIN preserves only the right table's unmatched rows.

questions.q: For Customers and Orders joined on CustomerId, where Kalpana (CustomerId 2) has no order and OrderId 200 (CustomerId 4) has no customer, which single query returns BOTH the customer without an order and the order without a customer?
o: SELECT * FROM Customers C INNER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId
SELECT * FROM Customers C FULL OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE C.CustomerId IS NULL OR O.OrderId IS NULL
SELECT * FROM Customers C LEFT OUTER JOIN Orders O ON O.CustomerId = C.CustomerId WHERE O.OrderId IS NULL
SELECT * FROM Customers C CROSS JOIN Orders O
questions.e: A FULL OUTER JOIN filtered by WHERE C.CustomerId IS NULL OR O.OrderId IS NULL returns both unmatched sides: the customer with no order and the order with no customer. The INNER JOIN returns only matches, the LEFT OUTER version returns only customers without orders, and CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product.

questions.q: A CROSS JOIN is also known by which name?
questions.e: A CROSS JOIN is referred to as the Cartesian product: for every left-table row, all right-table rows are returned. It uses no join condition, unlike an equi-join or natural join, and is unrelated to recursive/self joins.

questions.q: If the left table of a CROSS JOIN has 5 rows and the right table has 4 rows, how many rows are in the result?
questions.e: The number of rows in a CROSS JOIN result equals (rows in LEFT) * (rows in RIGHT) = 5 * 4 = 20. Adding the counts (9) or taking either single count (5, 1) misapplies the Cartesian-product rule.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of join statements required to join n tables in SQL?
questions.e: The minimum number of join statements needed to join n tables is (n - 1); the same logic used to join 2 tables (1 join) extends to more. The other counts overstate the number of joins required.

questions.q: In a SELF JOIN, how are the two references to the same table distinguished in the query?
o: By using a CROSS JOIN clause
By creating a temporary copy table
questions.e: A self-join uses the same table on both sides and distinguishes the two references with table aliases (e.g. p1 and p2). CROSS JOIN and DISTINCT serve other purposes, and no temporary copy table is created.

questions.q: Self-joins are usually used on tables that have which kind of relationship?
questions.e: Self-joins are typically used on tables with unary (recursive) relationships, where a table relates to itself. Many-to-many and ternary relationships involve multiple distinct tables, and a self-join specifically exploits a table's relationship to itself.

questions.q: Given People(person_id, person_state, ...), which condition set finds pairs of different people living in the same state via a self-join of aliases p1 and p2?
questions.e: Matching people in the same state requires p1.person_state = p2.person_state, and excluding a person paired with themselves requires p1.person_id != p2.person_id. Equating the ids or negating the state condition would break one of the two requirements.

questions.q: Placing an inner SELECT statement inside an outer query is called what?
questions.e: A subquery is an inner SELECT statement placed inside an outer query. A self-join joins a table to itself, and cross join / Cartesian product describe an unconditioned join, none of which involve a nested SELECT.

questions.q: In which of the following clauses can a subquery appear?
o: Only in the ORDER BY clause
Only in the GROUP BY clause
In the WHERE clause, the FROM clause, or the HAVING clause
questions.e: A subquery can be placed in a condition of the WHERE clause, as a 'table' in the FROM clause, or within the HAVING clause. It is not restricted to WHERE alone, and ORDER BY / GROUP BY are not the listed subquery locations.

questions.q: Which term describes a subquery that is executed only once for the entire outer query?
questions.e: A noncorrelated subquery is executed once for the entire outer query. A correlated subquery, by contrast, is executed once for each row returned by the outer query; 'recursive' and 'Cartesian' are not subquery classifications here.

questions.q: A correlated subquery is executed how many times relative to the outer query?
o: Once for the entire outer query
Never; it runs before the outer query
Once for each row returned by the outer query
Twice for the whole outer query
questions.e: A correlated subquery is executed once for each row returned by the outer query, because it depends on values from that row. Running once for the whole query describes a noncorrelated subquery instead.

questions.q: In a subquery such as 'WHERE CUSTOMER_ID IN (SELECT ... )', what does the IN operator do?
o: It joins the two tables on CUSTOMER_ID
It tests whether the row's CUSTOMER_ID value is included in the list returned by the subquery
It counts how many rows the subquery returns
It creates a Cartesian product of the two queries
questions.e: The IN operator tests membership: it checks whether a row's CUSTOMER_ID value is included in the list returned by the subquery. It does not perform a join, a count, or a Cartesian product.

questions.q: Which statement about joins and subqueries is correct?
o: A subquery can never be replaced by a join
A join can only return a single column
Some queries can be accomplished by either a join or a subquery
Subqueries are only allowed in the SELECT list
questions.e: Some queries can be accomplished by either a join or a subquery; the two approaches can produce equivalent results (e.g. finding customers who placed an order). Joins are not limited to one column, and subqueries appear in WHERE, FROM, or HAVING rather than only the SELECT list.

questions.q: An INNER JOIN of Customers and Orders on CustomerId is used to list the names of all customers who have at least one order. Which customers are EXCLUDED from this result?
o: Customers who have placed one or more orders
All customers, since INNER JOIN returns nothing
Customers who have no matching order in the Orders table
Orders that have no matching customer only
questions.e: An INNER JOIN returns only rows satisfying the join condition, so a customer with no matching order (e.g. Kalpana, CustomerId 2) is excluded. Customers with at least one order are kept, and the join does not return nothing; excluding unmatched orders is a separate effect on the Orders side.
